title: You Can’t Have It Both Ways: Concept Entanglement Limits Diffusion Model Unlearning

paper.title:
You Can’t Have It Both Ways:
Concept Entanglement Limits Diffusion Model Unlearning
paper.abstract: Abstract Concept unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models aims to suppress a target concept (e.g., horse ) while preserving related but distinct content (e.g., donkey ), yet existing methods either leak under indirect prompts or visibly degrade other concepts. We show that these failure modes stem from the geometry of concept representations rather than from any particular algorithm. Formalizing concepts as activation-space regions, we prove that the overlap between a target and other concepts lower-bounds the damage any robust erasure must inflict on them, with the trade-off scaling linearly in the degree of overlap. Across thirteen unlearning methods, including methods designed to preserve non-target concepts, no method achieves both strong erasure and strong neighbor preservation: STEREO nearly eliminates indirect leakage but cuts neighbor generation by more than 75%, while sparse inference-time methods preserve neighbors but leak. Damage increases with our overlap measure, monotonically so for STEREO; the κ \kappa -scaling reproduces on SDXL, and neighbor-selective damage recurs on FLUX. Perfect unlearning is the wrong target for entangled concepts; methods should be evaluated on the Pareto frontier our theorem establishes.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) have rapidly become the dominant generative paradigm for high-fidelity image synthesis, with deployments ranging from creative tools to commercial APIs. Privacy concerns and copyrights have motivated active research on concept unlearning ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) : given a trained model and an undesirable concept (e.g., an object category, an artistic style, or a specific identity), the goal is to suppress the concept while preserving the model’s general capabilities. In this work, we focus on object-category concepts, where benchmarks and detectors are most mature. A growing body of work has proposed methods for this task, ranging from fine-tuning-based approaches that permanently alter model weights ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) to inference-time interventions that block concept-specific activations without modifying the underlying model ( Li et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) . These methods are typically evaluated on two families of metrics: unlearning accuracy (UA), measuring whether the target concept has been successfully suppressed, and retain accuracy (RA), measuring whether the model’s performance on non-target concepts remains intact. A tacit assumption in this evaluation paradigm is that UA and RA can be optimized independently. However, our empirical evidence suggests this assumption is violated ( Section 3 ). Methods achieving strong erasure (high UA), such as STEREO ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) , often degrade generation quality on semantically related concepts (low RA). Methods with better retention, such as SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) , leave the target concept reachable through prompts that omit its name but supply correlated context (e.g., generating a horse from “a jockey at the racetrack”), a phenomenon we call concept leakage , resulting in low UA. These observations indicate a fundamental tension: unlearning and retention are inherently coupled when concepts share representational structure , a coupling visible directly in the model’s internal representations, where semantically related concepts ( horse / pony / donkey ) occupy overlapping regions of activation space while isolated concepts ( castle ) sit well-separated ( Figure 1 ). This shows that concept activation regions are real geometric structures whose overlap reflects semantic similarity, motivating our formal notion of concept activation regions in Section 4 1 1 1 The formal definition of concept activation regions is in Appendix A ; full empirical construction details and per-concept clustering statistics are in Appendix B . . Two failure modes follow from this geometry: concept leakage , where the target concept reappears under indirect prompts, and collateral forgetting , degraded generation of semantically related but distinct concepts. We show that these are not shortcomings of individual algorithms but dual symptoms of overlapping concept regions, and that any robust erasure method must trade them off. sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (i) We give a geometric account of concept entanglement, showing that the literature’s two failure modes, concept leakage and collateral forgetting, are dual symptoms of overlapping concept regions in cross-attention activation space (quantified by an entanglement coefficient κ ^ \hat{\kappa} ), rather than separate algorithmic shortcomings as treated in prior work ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ; Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) . (ii) Building on this account, we derive a geometric lower-bound for concept unlearning under empirically-verified assumptions: any method achieving ε \varepsilon -robust erasure must incur utility preservation error γ ≥ κ ⁡ ( 1 − ε ) / L \gamma\geq\kappa(1-\varepsilon)/L ( Theorem 4.6 ), with strict impossibility at ε = 0 \varepsilon=0 whenever κ > 0 \kappa>0 ( Corollary 4.8 ); this result reframes unlearning as a Pareto problem rather than a dual-objective one. (iii) We validate the predicted κ \kappa -scaled trade-off across thirteen methods on Stable Diffusion v1.4 (all methods on five targets, four methods on five additional targets that fill the intermediate κ ^ \hat{\kappa} range), with κ \kappa -scaling reproduced on SDXL, using a new Neighbor Preservation metric tied to the activation-level γ \gamma in our theorem.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Machine unlearning in diffusion models aims to remove a target concept c c (e.g., horse ) from a pretrained model 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} while preserving overall generative capabilities. The goal is an updated model 𝒟 θ ^ \mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}} that suppresses c c on target-associated prompts while maintaining quality on unrelated prompts, following prior work on concept erasure in diffusion models. Background on latent diffusion models is in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: Closed-form editing.
sections.text: UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) and RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) modify cross-attention projections through analytic updates, without gradient training. RECE additionally searches for embeddings that regenerate the target and removes them in closed form. Fine-tuning methods. A large body of work erase concepts by directly modifying the weights of a pretrained diffusion model. Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) Gandikota et al. (2023) uses negative guidance to align target-token prompts with a neutral anchor. Subsequent work improves the precision by editing cross-attention representations ( Wang et al., 2025 ) or updating salient concept-related parameters ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Wu and Harandi, 2024 ) . CPE ( Lee et al., 2025 ) trains residual attention gates with an anchoring loss, and TRUST ( Kori et al., 2026 ) selectively fine-tunes target-associated neurons under Hessian-based regularization. More recent robust methods such as AdvUnlearn Zhang et al. (2024) and STEREO Srivatsan et al. (2025) further defend against prompt-based regeneration attacks. However, these methods still largely define erasure through target tokens, prompts, or localized parameter subsets. They therefore suppress direct target prompts well, but struggle with concept leakage through correlated context; when made more aggressive, their edits can propagate through shared representations and cause collateral damage to semantic neighbors. Inference-time methods. A complementary line of work avoids modifying 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} and instead intervenes during generation by manipulating text embeddings ( Li et al., 2024 ) , projecting prompt tokens away from a target subspace (SAFREE, Yoon et al., 2025 ), adding safety guidance to the denoising process (SLD, Schramowski et al., 2023 ), inserting lightweight concept-blocking adapters ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , or ablating sparse-autoencoder features ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) . These methods are computationally efficient and often preserve broad model behavior. Intervening at inference time does not by itself make a method conservative: depending on how broadly the intervention displaces activations, these methods span the full range from strong erasure with substantial neighbor damage to strong preservation with residual leakage (Section 5.2 ).

sections.heading: Preservation-oriented methods.
sections.text: Several methods explicitly target the collateral damage we study. CPE anchors non-target concepts during erasure, TRUST restricts updates to target-associated neurons, and SAFREE adapts its filtering to preserve prompt fidelity. Adversarial preservation ( Bui et al., 2024 ) identifies and protects the concepts most sensitive to erasure, Receler ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) localize edits through lightweight erasers and LoRA fusion, and meta-unlearning ( Gao et al., 2025 ) prevents relearning of erased concepts. We evaluate CPE, TRUST, and SAFREE; they reach more favorable operating points but do not escape the trade-off (Section 5.2 ).

sections.heading: Positioning.
sections.text: That aggressive erasure degrades utility is well documented, and the preservation-oriented methods above aim to reduce it; localization work such as Zarei et al. (2026) identifies where concepts are represented. Neither models target-neighbor overlap or derives limits on unlearning. Our claim is narrower and structural: robust erasure necessarily degrades related concepts because their representations overlap, a limit we quantify through κ \kappa , prove unavoidable (Theorem 4.6 , Corollary 4.8 ), and turn into a frontier-based evaluation protocol. Across all three families, methods implicitly treat concepts as localized and independently suppressible; this assumption fails whenever activation regions overlap.

sections.heading: 3 Motivation
sections.text: Current concept unlearning methods are designed to suppress a concept token (e.g., “ horse ”) so as to remove the corresponding visual concept without substantially affecting other concepts. This design implicitly assumes that visual concepts are represented as localized, token-aligned features in the model’s joint text-image space. In this section, we present empirical evidence that this assumption fails: in practice, unlearning a target concept produces collateral damage to the concepts with which it is entangled. 2 2 2 We define entanglement formally in Section 4.1 based on activation regions in the model’s cross-attention space. The severity of this damage is coupled to both the strength of the erasure applied to the target concept and the extent of its entanglement with other concepts. This coupling is the phenomenon our theoretical framework analyzes in Section 4 . The training mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models make entanglement inevitable. First, diffusion models condition on prompt embeddings produced by text encoders that often exhibit bag-of-words behavior ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2022 ) . As a result, prompts that omit a concept token (e.g., horse ) but retain its characteristic context (e.g., jockey , saddle , racetrack ) can still induce activations associated with that concept (see Figure 7 ). This implies that the visual concept is not localized in a single token, but is instead distributed across multiple correlated context tokens. Second, semantically related concepts share much of this contextual structure (e.g., a horse in a field” vs. a donkey in a field” ), which leads to overlapping activation regions in the model’s internal representation space. Whether this overlap is already present in text space depends on the encoder. Under our estimator, SDXL’s CLIP text embeddings place nine of ten concepts in overlapping regions, whereas the T5 encoder of FLUX shows no measurable overlap for any of our five targets (Appendix L ). Entanglement in the denoiser therefore need not be inherited from the text encoder; its source and severity depend on both the text representation and the denoiser computation. We treat this comparison as descriptive rather than as a causal decomposition. Figure 2 illustrates an example of the trade-off due to this entanglement. It shows two unlearning methods using horse as the erasure target. Method that perform localized erasure (ESD Gandikota et al. (2023) ) successfully suppress generation when the target token is named, but regenerate the concept through indirect prompts that name only context words, which we call concept leakage . Methods that erase more aggressively (STEREO Srivatsan et al. (2025) ) suppress this leakage but produce visibly degraded outputs for some semantically similar concepts, such as donkey and zebra , that are entangled with the target concept (see Figure 1 ). We call this effect collateral damage . Table 1 quantifies this coupling. Averaged over five targets, STEREO achieves near-complete erasure (UA = 99.8 =99.8 , IRR = 3.5 =3.5 ) but retains only NP = 18.0 =18.0 on semantic neighbors, whereas SEOT preserves neighbors (NP = 85.1 =85.1 ) but leaves an indirect recovery rate of 24.5 24.5 . The damage also tracks entanglement: STEREO’s NP falls monotonically from 31.96 31.96 on castle ( κ ^ = 0.27 \hat{\kappa}=0.27 ) to 1.81 1.81 on dog ( κ ^ = 0.89 \hat{\kappa}=0.89 ; Section 5.3 ). Each row erases horse and is probed with three prompt types: Direct (mentions “ horse ”), Indirect (uses correlated context like jockey but omits “ horse ”), and Neighbor (semantically similar concept donkey ). ESD leaks horses through indirect prompts but preserves donkey; STEREO suppresses leakage but destroys donkey. We formalize this duality in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 4 The Robustness-Retention Trade-off: A Formal Impossibility Result
sections.text: We now formalize the coupling observed in Section 3 as a provable lower bound on the trade-off between erasure robustness and concept preservation. The governing quantity is the concept overlap coefficient κ \kappa , which measures the fraction of the target concept’s activation region shared with the remaining concepts.

sections.heading: 4.3 Consequences and Interpretation
sections.text: Limitations of simultaneous robust erasure and utility preservation. Based on Theorem 4.6 , simultaneous perfect erasure and perfect retention is infeasible whenever concepts are entangled: Corollary 4.8 (Impossibility result) . If κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) > 0 \kappa(c_{u},\rho)>0 , then no unlearning method can simultaneously achieve ε = 0 \varepsilon=0 (perfect erasure) and γ = 0 \gamma=0 (perfect neighbor preservation). Proof. Setting ε = 0 \varepsilon=0 in Eq. ( 8 ) gives γ ≥ κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) / L > 0 \gamma\geq\kappa(c_{u},\rho)/L>0 under the stated conditions. ∎ The Pareto frontier. Eq. ( 9 ) defines a feasibility boundary in the ( ε , γ ) (\varepsilon,\gamma) plane: no method can simultaneously achieve an erasure robustness below ε \varepsilon and a neighbor preservation error below γ \gamma unless the pair ( ε , γ ) (\varepsilon,\gamma) lies above the curve γ = κ ⋅ 1 − ε L . \gamma=\kappa\cdot\frac{1-\varepsilon}{L}. Different unlearning methods correspond to different operating points on or above this curve: aggressive methods achieve small ε \varepsilon at the cost of large γ \gamma , occupying the upper-left of the frontier; conservative methods accept large ε \varepsilon to maintain small γ \gamma , occupying the lower-right. In Section 5 , we verify that the empirically observed operating points across thirteen methods are consistent with this predicted boundary.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We design our experiments to answer three questions, each tied to a component of our contribution: Q1. Does the robustness-retention trade-off predicted by Theorem 4.6 manifest empirically across a broad set of unlearning methods? ( Section 5.2 ) Q2. Does the severity of the trade-off vary with the estimated entanglement coefficient κ ^ \hat{\kappa} , as predicted by the theorem’s dependence on κ \kappa ? ( Section 5.3 ) Q3. Do the Lipschitz continuity ( Assumption 4.4 ) and minimum displacement ( Assumption 4.5 ) assumptions underlying Theorem 4.6 hold empirically? ( Appendices E and D )

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Base model and target concepts. We use CompVis Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) as the base model 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} . Following ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , all generation uses 50 DDIM steps with guidance scale 7.5; full details in Appendix H . We select five target concepts spanning the range κ ^ ∈ [ 0.27 , 0.89 ] \hat{\kappa}\in[0.27,0.89] identified in Figure 1 : four high- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} animal-subtype concepts ( horse , dog , cat , bear , κ ^ ∈ [ 0.77 , 0.89 ] \hat{\kappa}\in[0.77,0.89] ) and one low- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} architectural concept ( castle , κ ^ = 0.27 \hat{\kappa}=0.27 ). Each target is evaluated against its discovered concept neighborhood and three control concepts ( Table 2 ); per-target prompt sets are detailed in Section I.1 . To densify the intermediate range we add five targets, snake , fish , tree , butterfly , and car ( κ ^ = 0.37 \hat{\kappa}=0.37 to 0.83 0.83 ), evaluated with four representative methods (Appendix J.6 ). Cross-architecture experiments on SDXL and FLUX are described in Appendix M . Unlearning methods. We benchmark 13 methods across three intervention families: closed-form editing (UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) ); fine-tuning (ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , SalUn ( Fan et al., 2023 ) , EDiff ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , CPE ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , TRUST ( Kori et al., 2026 ) , AdvUnlearn ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , STEREO ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) ); and inference-time methods (SEOT ( Li et al., 2024 ) , SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) , SLD ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , SAFREE ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) ). AdvUnlearn and STEREO incorporate adversarial training to target the aggressive-erasure end of the trade-off. Method-specific configurations are detailed in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Experimental data and sources.
sections.text: We use no existing labeled image test set. All images are generated by Stable Diffusion v1.4 or its unlearned variants from four controlled prompt families per target: direct prompts naming the target, indirect recovery prompts built from correlated context that excludes the target name, neighbor prompts naming concepts in 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{N}(c) , and control prompts naming unrelated concepts. Correlated context terms are mined from target-matched LAION caption text ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) ; LAION images are not used. For each target we generate around 200 images per prompt family (exact counts in Section H.3 ), all with 50 DDIM steps, guidance scale 7.5 7.5 , and fixed seeds shared across the original and unlearned models. Prompt files, seeds, the concept vocabulary, and discovered neighborhoods are released with the code (Appendices H and I ).

sections.heading: 5.3 Semantic Density Governs Trade-off Severity
sections.text: Theorem 4.6 predicts that trade-off severity scales with the entanglement coefficient κ \kappa : target concepts whose activation regions overlap substantially with other concepts should suffer greater collateral damage under robust erasure. We test this across five target concepts with estimated κ ^ \hat{\kappa} span from 0.27 0.27 ( castle ) to 0.89 0.89 ( dog ); see Figure 1 and Appendix C for the estimation procedure. κ ^ \hat{\kappa} predicts collateral damage on neighbors. Figure 3 plots NP against κ ^ \hat{\kappa} for the available method-concept pairs among the seven original methods, and the table on the right reports STEREO’s NP and in-domain retention ratio ordered by ascending κ ^ \hat{\kappa} . sections.text: On SDXL, whose cross-attention layers admit κ ^ \hat{\kappa} , ESD’s neighbor preservation decreases monotonically with entanglement: NP = 90.9 =90.9 , 85.0 85.0 , and 77.1 77.1 for cat , castle , and dog ( κ ^ SDXL = 0.65 \hat{\kappa}_{\text{SDXL}}=0.65 , 0.72 0.72 , 0.92 0.92 ; r s = − 1.0 r_{s}=-1.0 over three concepts). The most entangled target is also the least erased (UA = 77 =77 for dog versus 99 99 for cat ), so the ordering is not driven by erasure strength. Absolute κ ^ \hat{\kappa} shifts across architectures ( castle is 0.27 0.27 on SD v1.4 and 0.72 0.72 on SDXL), but κ ^ \hat{\kappa} and observed damage agree within each architecture. On the MMDiT model FLUX, joint text-image attention leaves no cross-attention block analogous to our probe, and a proxy estimator saturates near 1 1 even for unrelated control pairs, so κ \kappa -scaling on MMDiT remains untested. The phenomenon itself recurs: ESD on FLUX reduces NP to 35.6 35.6 to 40.5 40.5 on dog , cat , and castle while preserving unrelated controls (CP = 95.3 =95.3 to 98.9 98.9 ), i.e., neighbor-selective rather than global degradation (Appendix M ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that the tension between robust concept erasure and utility preservation in diffusion models is a structural consequence of representation geometry, not merely a limitation of existing methods. Theorem 4.6 establishes a κ \kappa -scaled lower bound on collateral damage, and our experiments show that existing methods, including those designed to preserve non-target concepts, occupy different points on the resulting robustness-retention frontier, and the frontier becomes steeper as κ ^ \hat{\kappa} increases.

sections.heading: Implications.
sections.text: Three consequences follow. First, κ ^ \hat{\kappa} is a pre-deployment diagnostic: estimated from base-model activations alone, it indicates which targets admit clean erasure and which require accepting collateral damage, before any unlearning is run ( Section J.7 ). Second, benchmarks should report erasure and retention jointly, on neighbor sets selected by activation overlap, because reporting either axis alone hides where a method sits on the frontier. Third, method design should be κ \kappa -aware: rather than suppressing broad adversarial subspaces, methods should restrict displacement to the directions needed for erasure.

sections.heading: Scope of empirical evaluation.
sections.text: All thirteen methods are evaluated on five targets on Stable Diffusion v1.4; five further targets are evaluated with four methods. Cross-architecture evidence is limited: SDXL covers three concepts with one method, and on FLUX we can show neighbor-selective damage but cannot resolve κ \kappa , so κ \kappa -scaling on MMDiT remains open. Our targets are object concepts; artistic styles, identities, and harmful-content concepts remain untested.

sections.heading: Theory and κ ^ \hat{\kappa} estimation.
sections.text: Theorem 4.6 applies to any unlearning mechanism, but its constants are effective ones: L L captures the full network, including skip connections, and is estimated only for the prompt variations of Appendix E . κ ^ \hat{\kappa} is an empirical lower-bound proxy for κ \kappa whose absolute value depends on the probe layer, the denoising timestep (e.g., κ ^ ​ ( castle ) = 0.77 \hat{\kappa}(\texttt{castle})=0.77 at step 10), and the candidate pool; our claims rely on its ranking, which is stable across the settings we test. The text-space comparison is not a causal decomposition of where entanglement arises.

sections.heading: A.1 Background: latent diffusion models
sections.text: We briefly introduce the latent diffusion notation used throughout the paper, since our analysis of concept activation regions and unlearning-induced perturbations is defined over the model’s latent, text-conditioned denoising process. Text-to-image latent diffusion models. We consider a text-to-image latent diffusion model (LDM) of the form introduced in Stable Diffusion [ Rombach et al., 2022 ] . An input image 𝐱 ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X} is first mapped by a pretrained variational autoencoder encoder E E into a latent representation 𝐳 = E ⁡ ( x ) ∈ 𝒵 \mathbf{z}=E(x)\in\mathcal{Z} , and reconstructed by a decoder V : 𝒵 → 𝒳 V:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathcal{X} . Given a latent 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , the forward diffusion process corrupts it with Gaussian noise to obtain 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} at timestep t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} . A time-conditioned U-Net ϵ θ \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} is then trained to predict the noise ϵ \boldsymbol{\epsilon} added to 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} . In text-conditioned generation, a prompt p ∈ 𝒫 p\in\mathcal{P} is encoded by a text encoder f ψ f_{\psi} into text features 𝐞 p = f ψ ​ ( p ) \mathbf{e}_{p}=f_{\psi}(p) , and these features condition the U-Net through cross-attention layers. The standard latent diffusion objective is ℒ LDM = 𝔼 x , ϵ , t ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐞 p ) ‖ 2 2 ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LDM}}=\mathbb{E}_{x,\epsilon,t}\left[\left\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{e}_{p})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (11) where ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) At inference time, generation starts from Gaussian noise and iteratively denoises toward a clean latent, which is finally decoded into an image.

sections.heading: Appendix B Empirical Validation of Concept Activation Regions
sections.text: This section provides empirical support for Definition A.1 by showing that the cross-attention activations used in our formalization form coherent geometric clusters in practice.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: To verify that concept activation regions are well-defined empirical objects, we extract cross-attention activations from Stable Diffusion v1.4 at the mid-block layer ( mid_block.attentions.0 ) at step t ∗ = 25 t^{*}{=}25 of 50 DDIM steps for 10 concepts, each prompted with 50 shared templates differing only in the concept word. horse , pony , donkey , deer , dog , cat , bear , car , truck , and castle . This visualization pool is chosen to be illustrative rather than comprehensive: it deliberately spans three semantically distinct domains (animals, vehicles, architecture) so that the qualitative geometry of concept regions (semantically related concepts clustering while distinct domains separate) is visually apparent. Several concepts in this pool ( deer , car , truck ) are not part of the evaluation vocabulary in Table 5 ; they appear only to anchor the visualization’s domain diversity. Conversely, κ ^ \hat{\kappa} -estimation and all CLIP-based evaluation metrics use the full 65 65 -concept pool of Table 5 , of which the visualization pool is not a strict subset. For each concept, we generate 50 prompts using a shared set of templates that differ only in the concept word, so that differences in activation primarily reflect the concept token rather than unrelated prompt variation. For each prompt p p , we compute the activation 𝚽 θ ​ ( p ) = A θ ​ ( 𝐞 p , ℓ ∗ , t ∗ ) ∈ ℋ , \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\theta}(p)\;=\;\mathrm{A}_{\theta}(\mathbf{e}_{p},\ell^{*},t^{*})\in\mathcal{H}, (14) flatten the resulting cross-attention tensor into a vector in ℋ \mathcal{H} , and project all activations to two dimensions using UMAP for visualization.

sections.heading: Observations.
sections.text: Figure 1 shows that activations induced by prompts containing the same concept form concentrated local clusters, rather than being arbitrarily scattered in activation space. This supports the view that each concept corresponds to a coherent region in the model’s internal representation space. The figure also reveals non-uniform distances between concepts. Some concepts occupy nearby regions (for example, horse , pony , and donkey form a tight cluster), while others, such as castle , are clearly separated from the animal concepts. Importantly, we do not use these visualizations to infer semantic relatedness from scratch. Rather, the figure shows that the activation geometry is structured and that concepts commonly regarded as related in the data domain tend to induce nearby activations under shared prompt templates. These results do not by themselves prove overlap in the strict set-theoretic sense used later in Section 4. Instead, they provide empirical evidence for the weaker claim needed to motivate our definitions: concept-conditioned activations are localized, stable enough to visualize, and often organized into neighboring regions rather than isolated points. This makes it meaningful to model a concept through an activation region ℛ c \mathcal{R}_{c} and to reason about neighborhood structure in the induced activation space.

sections.heading: Choice of probe layer and timestep.
sections.text: We probe the cross-attention output at mid_block.attentions.0 at denoising step t ∗ = 25 t^{*}=25 of 50 50 throughout Appendices B , C , D and E , and at up_blocks.1.attentions.1 (same timestep) for the direct displacement measurements in Appendix K . The probe layer ℓ ∗ \ell^{*} is a parameter of our framework ( Definition A.1 ), not a property of the model, and Theorem 4.6 holds for any chosen ( ℓ ∗ , t ∗ ) (\ell^{*},t^{*}) at which Assumptions 4.4 and 4.5 are satisfied. We selected mid-block as the default probe based on a sensitivity analysis ( Section C.2 ) over six candidate cross-attention layers spanning the U-Net depth: the κ ^ \hat{\kappa} ordering across our five target concepts is stable across all probed layers ( r s ≥ 0.80 r_{s}\geq 0.80 vs. mid-block), but mid-block produces the cleanest bimodal separation between high- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} and low- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} concepts and the tightest within-cluster spread among the animal subtypes. Step t ∗ = 25 t^{*}=25 (the midpoint of the DDIM trajectory) corresponds to the regime in which large-scale layout and object identity are committed in latent diffusion models. The up-block layer in Appendix K was selected because it lies downstream of the cross-attention edits applied by fine-tuning methods and therefore reflects the cumulative effect of those edits; Section C.2 confirms that the κ ^ \hat{\kappa} ranking at this layer is consistent with mid-block.

sections.heading: Appendix C Estimation of the Entanglement Coefficient κ ^ \hat{\kappa}
sections.text: The entanglement coefficient κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) \kappa(c_{u},\rho) defined in Definition 4.1 involves the volume of high-dimensional activation regions, which is intractable to compute directly. We therefore estimate κ \kappa via a sample-based procedure that restricts the overlap measurement to a discovered semantic neighborhood 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) ⊆ 𝒞 ∖ { c u } \mathcal{N}(c_{u})\subseteq\mathcal{C}\setminus\{c_{u}\} rather than the full union over remaining concepts. Because 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) \mathcal{N}(c_{u}) is a subset of the union appearing in Definition 4.1 , this neighborhood-restricted estimate is a lower bound on κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) \kappa(c_{u},\rho) . We argue, and verify in Section C.1 , that this lower bound is tight in practice: across the five targets, the activation overlap with non-neighbors is negligible, so the union over 𝒞 ∖ { c u } \mathcal{C}\setminus\{c_{u}\} is dominated by the union over 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) \mathcal{N}(c_{u}) . Throughout this section we work with cosine distance d cos ​ ( 𝐚 , 𝐛 ) = 1 − ⟨ 𝐚 , 𝐛 ⟩ / ( ‖ 𝐚 ‖ ​ ‖ 𝐛 ‖ ) d_{\cos}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=1-\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\rangle/(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|) , which is the standard choice in representation analysis: it is invariant to activation magnitude (which is dominated by token-position effects under mean-pooling) and captures directional similarity, the property most closely tied to concept identity. The centroid-distance matrix used to motivate neighborhood structure in Section 4 ( Figure 4 ) uses the same metric, ensuring internal consistency between our motivation and our formalization.

sections.text: For each concept c c , we generate images from 50 shared prompt templates (differing only in the concept word) using the base model (Stable Diffusion v1.4) with DDIM sampling (50 steps, guidance scale 7.5). sections.heading: On the use of centroid distance as a proxy.
sections.text: The centroid cosine distance plays a different role from κ ^ \hat{\kappa} itself, and the two should not be conflated. Definition 4.1 is stated in terms of the volume of fattened activation regions, whose membership is determined by an infimum over per-sample distances (the closed ρ \rho -neighborhood ℛ c ( ρ ) \mathcal{R}_{c}^{(\rho)} ). The centroid, by contrast, is a single average summary of each region. Centroid distance is used only for neighborhood discovery ( Definition C.1 ), an upstream step of deciding which pairs of concepts are close enough to warrant an overlap measurement. We use it here for two reasons. First, it is a stable summary statistic that degrades gracefully under the finite-sample, high-dimensional regime in which we estimate activation regions. Second, an outlier-robust statistic at this stage is conservative: a concept that is filtered out of 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) \mathcal{N}(c_{u}) contributes zero to the resulting estimator, so under-inclusion only weakens the bound. The estimator κ ^ \hat{\kappa} is therefore a lower bound on κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) \kappa(c_{u},\rho) both because 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) ⊆ 𝒞 ∖ { c u } \mathcal{N}(c_{u})\subseteq\mathcal{C}\setminus\{c_{u}\} and because the discovery step itself is conservative. Empirical comparisons against the bound of Theorem 4.6 therefore remain valid. The κ ^ \hat{\kappa} statistic itself does not use centroid distance. As specified in the overlap estimation step above, κ ^ \hat{\kappa} is computed via a nearest-neighbor estimator: for each activation sample 𝐚 ∈ 𝒮 c u \mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{S}_{c_{u}} , we check whether there exists any sample 𝐛 \mathbf{b} from any concept in 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) \mathcal{N}(c_{u}) with d cos ​ ( 𝐚 , 𝐛 ) ≤ ρ d_{\cos}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\leq\rho . This is the natural finite-sample analogue of the fattened-region membership condition 𝐚 ∈ ℛ c ′ ( ρ ) \mathbf{a}\in\mathcal{R}_{c^{\prime}}^{(\rho)} (with the radius ρ \rho converted to cosine units, see “On the relationship between cosine and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} metrics” above), and the fraction of target samples satisfying this condition is a Monte Carlo estimate of the volume ratio in Definition 4.1 restricted to 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) \mathcal{N}(c_{u}) . The centroid-distance visualization in Figure 4 therefore serves only as an auxiliary consistency check: blocks of small centroid distance should coincide with the discovered 𝒩 ⁡ ( c u ) \mathcal{N}(c_{u}) , and the high- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} targets should sit inside such blocks.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Under this estimator, κ ^ ​ ( c u ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \hat{\kappa}(c_{u})\in[0,1] captures the sample-level coverage of the target region by its neighbors. The results in Figure 1 exhibit a bimodal structure. The four animal-subtype concepts embedded in dense semantic neighborhoods, dog ( κ ^ = 0.89 \hat{\kappa}=0.89 ), bear ( κ ^ = 0.82 \hat{\kappa}=0.82 ), horse ( κ ^ = 0.81 \hat{\kappa}=0.81 ), and cat ( κ ^ = 0.77 \hat{\kappa}=0.77 ), exhibit the highest overlap, consistent with their small inter-centroid distances to fine-grained subtypes ( Figure 4 ). Under our procedure, these concepts each have multiple discovered neighbors, and individual samples from these neighbors fall within the fattening radius ρ \rho of a substantial fraction of target samples. The high overlap is also robust to which neighbors are included: in the horse pool, several individual neighbors ( mare , pony , stallion ) each cover 60 to 80% of target samples on their own, and the union across all seven discovered neighbors saturates at κ ^ = 0.81 \hat{\kappa}=0.81 , indicating that overlap is supported by a representational manifold shared across the equine subtype family rather than driven by a single sensitive neighbor choice. The architectural concept castle , by contrast, exhibits substantially lower overlap ( κ ^ = 0.27 \hat{\kappa}=0.27 ) despite having six discovered neighbors within δ c u \delta_{c_{u}} . The distinction is qualitative: castle’s neighbors are semantically related but represent distinct architectural types rather than fine-grained subtypes of a shared category. They occupy nearby but non-overlapping regions of activation space, so the centroid distances cross the δ c u \delta_{c_{u}} threshold while individual sample-level overlap remains limited. Controls like jellyfish , melon , police car are correctly filtered out by the δ c u \delta_{c_{u}} step across all five targets and contribute zero to κ ^ \hat{\kappa} , confirming that the estimator is not driven by pool-wide sample density. This bimodal structure, high- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} animal subtypes clustered in [ 0.77 , 0.89 ] [0.77,0.89] and moderate- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} architecture at 0.27 0.27 reflects a property of the model’s internal representations at the probed layer: text-to-image diffusion models represent fine-grained subtypes of a common taxonomic category (breeds of dog, equine subtypes) as overlapping regions of a shared activation manifold, while distinct-but-related concepts in other domains maintain more separable representations. Theorem 4.6 predicts that the collateral damage from erasing high- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} concepts will be substantially greater than from erasing low- κ ^ \hat{\kappa} concepts; we verify this prediction in Section 5 . κ ^ \hat{\kappa} measures activation-space overlap, not semantic similarity. A natural concern is whether κ ^ \hat{\kappa} proxies for some other concept-level property such as semantic category (animal vs. architecture). Our estimator ( Appendix C ) is computed from sample-level overlap of activation regions, not from category labels or human-judged similarity. Castle ( κ ^ = 0.27 \hat{\kappa}=0.27 ) and the four animal concepts ( κ ^ ∈ [ 0.77 , 0.89 ] \hat{\kappa}\in[0.77,0.89] ) differ in κ ^ \hat{\kappa} not because they belong to different taxonomic categories but because castle’s discovered neighbors occupy sub-regions of activation space despite being semantically related, while animal subtypes densely overlap their target’s region.

sections.heading: Appendix D Empirical Validation of the Minimum Displacement Assumption
sections.text: This section provides empirical support for Assumption 4.5 by measuring the activation displacement induced by six unlearning methods and verifying that the displacement propagates to semantic neighbors in proportion to their overlap with the target concept.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We extract cross-attention activations at mid_block.attentions.0 at step t ∗ = 25 t^{*}{=}25 of 50 DDIM steps from six unlearning methods applied to erase horse : ESD, EDiff, SalUn, TRUST, AdvUnlearn, and STEREO. For each method, we compare activations between the original model 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} and the concept-erased model 𝒟 θ ^ \mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}} under matched random seeds, so that observed differences reflect the unlearning edit rather than sampling variance. We measure mean displacement ‖ Φ θ ^ ​ ( p ) − Φ θ ​ ( p ) ‖ 2 \|\Phi_{\hat{\theta}}(p)-\Phi_{\theta}(p)\|_{2} across three prompt categories: • Target prompts containing the erased concept ( horse ); • Neighbor prompts containing semantically related concepts ( pony , donkey , deer ); • Control prompts containing semantically isolated concepts ( castle , car ). For each prompt category, we use the same 50 shared templates as in Appendix B , differing only in the concept word. Activations are mean-pooled across spatial and token dimensions to produce a single vector per prompt, so the absolute magnitudes reported here are token-averaged and not directly comparable to the unpooled, full-tensor displacement values reported at a different layer in Appendix K ( Table 14 ); the two appendices probe different facets of the propagation mechanism: this one establishes the ordering Δ target , Δ neighbor > Δ control \Delta_{\mathrm{target}},\Delta_{\mathrm{neighbor}}>\Delta_{\mathrm{control}} within a single target, while Appendix K establishes the κ ^ \hat{\kappa} -scaling of Δ neighbor \Delta_{\mathrm{neighbor}} across targets. Figure 5 reports the mean displacement by method and prompt category. Two patterns emerge. First, all six methods produce measurable target displacement (approximately 6 6 to 16 16 in mean-pooled activation L 2 L_{2} distance), with TRUST producing the largest mean displacement. This pattern is consistent with the minimum-displacement assumption in Assumption 4.5 . The magnitudes show how strongly each edit perturbs the probed representation; displacement alone does not measure erasure quality. TRUST, whose update is gradient-based, produces the largest target displacement ( 15.82 ± 3.82 15.82\pm 3.82 ) and displaces neighbors ( 8.82 ± 4.88 8.82\pm 4.88 ) far more than controls ( 3.10 ± 1.36 3.10\pm 1.36 ), confirming that Assumption 4.5 and the propagation mechanism hold for gradient-based fine-tuning. Second, the displacement propagates to semantic neighbors: for every method, Δ neighbor ≥ Δ control \Delta_{\mathrm{neighbor}}\geq\Delta_{\mathrm{control}} with the gap ranging from 0.9 0.9 (SalUn) to 6.9 6.9 (STEREO). This gap is the empirical signature of the propagation mechanism in Theorem 4.6 : displacement within ℛ c u \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}} leaks into overlapping neighbor regions in proportion to κ \kappa , causing greater collateral displacement for high- κ \kappa neighbors than for low- κ \kappa controls. EraseDiff exhibits the smallest cross-category variation, suggesting it operates in a low-selectivity regime where κ \kappa -modulated propagation falls below our measurement granularity. Third, STEREO is the only method for which Δ neighbor > Δ target \Delta_{\mathrm{neighbor}}>\Delta_{\mathrm{target}} , while simultaneously achieving the lowest control displacement ( 2.1 2.1 ). This produces a propagation gap of 6.9 6.9 , the largest of all six methods. This pattern is consistent with our analysis of STEREO in Remark F.2 : by suppressing the entire subspace spanned by the adversarial tokens v 1 ∗ , v 2 ∗ v_{1}^{*},v_{2}^{*} rather than the target alone, STEREO displaces neighbor concepts that lie within this shared subspace by even more than the target itself, while leaving semantically isolated concepts largely intact. These measurements support two claims central to our analysis. The uniform presence of nontrivial target displacement validates the precondition of Assumption 4.5 . The systematic neighbor, control gap, and STEREO’s amplified version of it, validate the propagation claim in Step 2 of the proof: methods are not merely displacing the target in isolation but are displacing overlapping regions of activation space, with the magnitude of this collateral displacement modulated by the geometric overlap κ \kappa predicted by Theorem 4.6 . The robust prediction of the theorem is the ordering Δ neighbor > Δ control \Delta_{\mathrm{neighbor}}>\Delta_{\mathrm{control}} within each method and its scaling with κ \kappa across concept types, not specific numerical values. Target prompts (blue) confirm Assumption 4.5 : erasure requires measurable displacement. Neighbor prompts (orange) are displaced more than control prompts (green) for all methods, consistent with the propagation mechanism in Theorem 4.6 .

sections.heading: Appendix E Empirical Validation of the Lipschitz Assumption
sections.text: This section provides empirical support for Assumption 4.4 by measuring the relationship between activation distance and change in concept generation probability under natural prompt variations, and verifying that the observed relationship is consistent with a Lipschitz bound with a small empirical constant.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: For each of the ten concepts in Appendix B , we construct a set of prompt pairs ( p b , p v ) (p_{b},p_{v}) where p b p_{b} is a base prompt containing the concept and p v p_{v} is a variant prompt obtained by one of four perturbations at increasing semantic distance: • Synonym substitution: replacing the concept word with a close synonym (e.g., horse → \to stallion ); • Scene change: altering the background or setting while preserving the concept (e.g., “in a field” → \to “on a beach”); • Related concept: substituting a semantically related concept (e.g., horse → \to pony ); • Unrelated concept: substituting an unrelated concept (e.g., horse → \to castle ). For each pair, we extract cross-attention activations at mid_block.attentions.0 (step t ∗ = 25 t^{*}{=}25 ) and compute the activation distance ‖ 𝚽 θ ​ ( p v ) − 𝚽 θ ​ ( p b ) ‖ 2 \|\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\theta}(p_{v})-\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\theta}(p_{b})\|_{2} . We then generate images from each prompt and compute the concept generation probability P ⁡ ( p ) P(p) using a CLIP-based classifier aligned to the base concept. The quantity of interest is the pair ( ‖ Φ θ ​ ( p v ) − Φ θ ​ ( p b ) ‖ 2 , | P ⁡ ( p v ) − P ⁡ ( p b ) | ) \bigl(\|\Phi_{\theta}(p_{v})-\Phi_{\theta}(p_{b})\|_{2},\;|P(p_{v})-P(p_{b})|\bigr) . This experiment validates the case θ ′ = θ ′′ = θ \theta^{\prime}=\theta^{\prime\prime}=\theta of Assumption 4.4 . Figure 6 plots the concept probability change against the activation distance for all prompt pairs, colored by perturbation type. Two patterns emerge. First, the four perturbation types occupy approximately nested bands of activation distance, with synonyms producing the smallest displacements, scene changes and related-concept substitutions producing intermediate displacements, and unrelated-concept substitutions producing the largest. Second, the change in concept probability scales roughly linearly with activation distance within each band, with no prompt pair exceeding a bound of the form | P ⁡ ( p v ) − P ⁡ ( p b ) | ≤ L ^ ​ ‖ Φ θ ​ ( p v ) − Φ θ ​ ( p b ) ‖ 2 |P(p_{v})-P(p_{b})|\leq\hat{L}\,\|\Phi_{\theta}(p_{v})-\Phi_{\theta}(p_{b})\|_{2} for empirical constant L ^ ≈ 0.174 \hat{L}\approx 0.174 . We emphasize that the empirical constant L ^ \hat{L} should be read as a conservative upper bound for this specific layer, timestep, and set of concepts, not as a universal property of Stable Diffusion. Varying the probe layer, the timestep, or the CLIP classifier would likely change the numerical value. The claim we extract from this measurement is weaker and more robust: the concept probability mapping is empirically smooth as a function of activation distance, with no observed violations of the Lipschitz condition across hundreds of prompt pairs spanning four perturbation types. This is the regularity our proof requires. For illustration, combining L ^ ≈ 0.174 \hat{L}\approx 0.174 with ε = 0.05 \varepsilon=0.05 yields a minimum displacement bound of Δ ≥ ( 1 − ε ) / L ^ ≈ 5.5 \Delta\geq(1-\varepsilon)/\hat{L}\approx 5.5 , consistent with the target displacements observed in Appendix D . Each point is a (base, variant) prompt pair; the x x -axis shows activation distance and the y y -axis shows the change in CLIP-based concept probability. Points are colored by semantic distance from the base prompt (green: synonyms; blue: scene changes; orange: related concepts; red: unrelated concepts). All points lie below the empirical bound L ^ = 0.174 \hat{L}=0.174 (dotted line), supporting Assumption 4.4 .

sections.heading: The role of κ \kappa : why the trade-off severity varies.
sections.text: The overlap coefficient κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) \kappa(c_{u},\rho) determines the slope of the Pareto frontier and hence how severe the trade-off is for a given target concept. Concepts embedded in semantically dense neighborhoods (e.g., horse among other animals, or Monet among Impressionist styles) have large κ \kappa and face a steep trade-off. Concepts that are semantically isolated have small κ \kappa and can be erased with less collateral damage. This provides actionable guidance: the difficulty of unlearning a concept depends not only on the method but on the semantic density of its neighborhood . Remark F.1 (Tightness of the bound) . The bound in Theorem 4.6 is tight when the overlap region 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is exactly a κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ CLOSE \kappa(c_{u},\rho ) fraction of ℛ c u ( ρ ) \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}}^{(\rho)} and the displacement field induced by the unlearning edit is uniform over ℛ c u ( ρ ) \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}}^{(\rho)} . In practice, displacement is typically non-uniform, since methods may suppress some directions more aggressively than others, in which case the bound is conservative. Characterizing the displacement geometry more precisely is an interesting direction for future work.

sections.heading: Reading existing methods as operating points on the frontier.
sections.text: We now apply this framing to specific unlearning methods, interpreting their empirical behavior as distinct operating points on the predicted Pareto frontier. The discussion is interpretive rather than derivational: we identify where on the frontier each method sits and connect this to the method’s mechanism. Remark F.2 (Why STEREO achieves robustness at the cost of retention) . STEREO [ Srivatsan et al., 2025 ] achieves robustness by learning adversarial token embeddings v 1 ∗ , v 2 ∗ v_{1}^{*},v_{2}^{*} that lie near the hardest-to-suppress directions of ℛ c u \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}} , then using a compositional objective to suppress the entire subspace spanned by these directions. This broad suppression corresponds to a large displacement Δ \Delta across ℛ c u \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}} , which by Theorem 4.6 directly implies large collateral displacement in ℛ c ′ \mathcal{R}_{c^{\prime}} for all neighbors c ′ c^{\prime} with κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) > 0 \kappa(c_{u},\rho)>0 . Our empirical observation that donkey and zebra generation degrades after horse erasure with STEREO ( Section 3 ) is consistent with this prediction. Remark F.3 (Why SAeUron preserves neighbors but remains vulnerable) . SAeUron [ Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ] achieves unlearning by identifying a small number of sparse autoencoder features ( τ c \tau_{c} features per concept) that are highly specific to the target concept, then ablating only those features during inference. Because the intervention is restricted to a sparse set of concept-specific features rather than applied across the full activation region ℛ c u \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}} , the effective displacement Δ \Delta is small and concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. This limits collateral damage to neighbors (small γ \gamma ), explaining SAeUron’s superior retention performance in sequential unlearning. However, the sparsity of the intervention also means that portions of ℛ c u \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}} remain unsuppressed, precisely the portions reachable through indirect correlated prompts, consistent with the concept leakage observed in Section 3 . In the language of our framework, SAeUron achieves small γ \gamma at the cost of large ε \varepsilon . Remark F.4 (Intervention breadth determines the operating point) . More generally, a method’s operating point on the ( ε , γ ) (\varepsilon,\gamma) frontier is set by how broadly it displaces activations across ℛ c u \mathcal{R}_{c_{u}} , not by whether it edits weights or intervenes at inference time. Methods that displace activations broadly, whether by fine-tuning (SalUn, AdvUnlearn, STEREO) or at inference time (SLD), achieve small ε \varepsilon at the cost of larger γ \gamma . Methods whose intervention is narrow, such as SEOT and SAeUron, achieve small γ \gamma but leave larger ε \varepsilon because the intervention does not cover the full activation region. This is a direct consequence of Theorem 4.6 : the effective displacement Δ \Delta is the lever, and methods differ in how broadly they apply it.

sections.heading: Appendix G Proof of Theorem 4.6
Remark on metric compatibility.
sections.text: The proof uses the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} metric throughout because Assumption 4.4 is stated in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} . Our κ ^ \hat{\kappa} estimator ( Appendix C ) instead uses cosine distance to characterize region membership. These two choices are compatible at the level of the geometric objects in the bound: for unit-normalized activations, ‖ 𝐚 − 𝐛 ‖ 2 2 = 2 ​ d cos ​ ( 𝐚 , 𝐛 ) \|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\|_{2}^{2}=2\,d_{\cos}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) , so the two metrics induce the same topology on the activation sphere and define the same fattened regions ℛ c ( ρ ) \mathcal{R}_{c}^{(\rho)} and entanglement coefficient κ ⁡ ( c u , ρ ) \kappa(c_{u},\rho) up to a monotone re-parameterization of the radius ρ \rho . This re-parameterization is absorbed into the choice of ρ \rho in our empirical κ ^ \hat{\kappa} estimator. Consequently, estimating κ \kappa via cosine distance while applying the theoretical bound under an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} Lipschitz assumption is internally consistent: the bound’s set-theoretic content (volume overlap of ρ \rho -neighborhoods) transfers between metrics, while the Lipschitz constant L L remains tied to the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} formulation in which Assumption 4.4 is stated.

sections.heading: Appendix H Implementation Details
sections.text: Here we introduce the implementation of each unlearning method used in Section 5 , including hyperparameters, training protocols, and compute budgets. All methods are applied to CompVis Stable Diffusion v1.4 [ Rombach et al., 2022 ] . The full implementation, including code, prompt CSVs, and evaluation scripts, is available at our public repository: https://github.com/Jazzssmine/concept-entangle

sections.heading: H.1 Method-Specific Hyperparameters
sections.text: We group the 13 benchmarked methods into three mechanism families. Closed-form editing methods (UCE, RECE) modify model weights through analytic updates. Fine-tuning methods (ESD, SalUn, EDiff, CPE, TRUST, AdvUnlearn, STEREO) modify model weights through gradient-based optimization. Inference-time methods (SEOT, SAeUron, SLD, SAFREE) intervene during generation without permanently modifying the base model. AdvUnlearn and STEREO additionally incorporate adversarial training, explicitly targeting the aggressive-erasure end of the trade-off; their inclusion tests whether robustness gains incur measurable cost to neighbor preservation. Unless otherwise noted, we use the hyperparameters specified in each method’s original publication. We document deviations and choices not fully specified by the original papers in the per-method descriptions below.

sections.heading: UCE [ Gandikota et al., 2024 ] .
sections.text: Unified Concept Editing uses closed-form updates to text-to-image attention projections to erase target concepts without gradient training. Configuration: guide concept unconditional , erase scale 1.0 , preserve scale 1.0 , regularization λ \lambda 0.5 , no explicit preserve concepts; each concept is erased independently.

sections.heading: RECE [ Gong et al., 2024 ] .
sections.text: Reliable and Efficient Concept Erasure iteratively discovers embeddings that recover the target concept and removes their effect through closed-form cross-attention edits. Configuration: initialized from base SD v1.4, edit epochs 1 , erase scale 1.0 , preserve scale 0.1 , λ \lambda 0.1 , adversarial-embedding regularization 0.1 , guide concept unconditional .

sections.heading: ESD [ Gandikota et al., 2023 ] .
sections.text: Erased Stable Diffusion fine-tunes the cross-attention layers to suppress the target concept via a negative-guidance objective. We use the ESD-sd (stable-diffusion) variant. Configuration: learning rate 5e-5 , training steps 200 , negative guidance scale η = 5 \eta=\textbf{5} , batch size 1 . Training uses the target concept name as the single forget prompt. For the cross-architecture experiments ( Appendix M ), we adapt ESD to each backbone. On SDXL (base-1.0) we use the ESD-x variant, which fine-tunes only the U-Net cross-attention layers ( attn2 query, key, value, and output projections; about 546M parameters). Configuration: Adam, learning rate 2e-4 , training steps 200 , batch size 1 , negative guidance scale η = 1 \eta=\textbf{1} . On FLUX.1-schnell we use a stricter ESD-x variant that fine-tunes only the attention key and value projections ( to_k , to_v ) in all 19 joint and 38 single transformer blocks (about 1.08B parameters), keeping the text-side projections ( add_k_proj , add_v_proj ) frozen. Configuration: learning rate 1e-5 , training steps 500 , negative guidance scale η = 2 \eta=\textbf{2} .

sections.heading: SalUn [ Fan et al., 2023 ] .
sections.text: Saliency-guided Unlearning identifies salient weights via gradient magnitudes and applies random labeling on the forget set to those weights only. We use saliency threshold sparsity 0.5 , forget-set size 800 , learning rate 1e-5 , and training epochs 5 . The forget and retain sets consist of 800 target and 800 non-target images generated by Stable Diffusion v1.4.

sections.heading: EDiff [ Wu et al., 2024 ] .
sections.text: EraseDiff fine-tunes the UNet using a bi-level optimization that explicitly balances erasure and retention objectives. Configuration: learning rate 1e-5 , inner steps per outer update 2 , total outer iterations 300 .

sections.heading: CPE [ Lee et al., 2025 ]
sections.text: Concept Pinpoint Eraser trains nonlinear residual attention gates with an anchoring loss to suppress target concepts while preserving other concepts. Configuration: 5 stages of 450 iterations each (stage 1 uses 4 × 4\times the iterations and 10 × 10\times the learning rate), learning rate 3e-5 , gate rank 16 , erasure guidance 0.3 , PAL weight 1e5 , noise 1e-3 ; adversarial learning with learning rate 1e-2 , 450 iterations, and 16 added prompts per stage.

sections.heading: TRUST [ Kori et al., 2026 ]
sections.text: TRUST dynamically identifies target-associated neurons and selectively fine-tunes them with Hessian-based regularization. Configuration: concept neurons are heads whose | z ​ -score | > |z\text{-score}|> 2.0 on the CLIP-loss attribution; learning rate 1e-4 , batch size 2 , 2 epochs of 60 steps (final checkpoint), 25 sampling steps for neuron localization.

sections.heading: AdvUnlearn [ Zhang et al., 2024 ] .
sections.text: Adversarial Unlearning augments the erasure objective with adversarial prompt generation to improve robustness against indirect concept recovery. We use adversarial prompt budget 30 per training step, adversarial learning rate 1e-3 , main-model learning rate 1e-5 , and training steps 1000 . The attack prompts are updated per training steps.

sections.heading: STEREO [ Srivatsan et al., 2025 ] .
sections.text: STEREO proceeds in two phases: a Search for Trainable Embeddings via RObust optimization (STE) phase that learns adversarial token embeddings v 1 ∗ , v 2 ∗ v_{1}^{*},v_{2}^{*} , followed by a Robust Erasure via Orthogonalization (REO) phase that suppresses the subspace spanned by these embeddings. STE phase: 200 steps, learning rate 5e-6 . REO phase: 200 steps, learning rate 2e-5 , K = 2 K=\textbf{2} adversarial embeddings per target.

sections.heading: SEOT [ Li et al., 2024 ] .
sections.text: Soft Embedding Optimization for Target-concept erasure modifies the text embedding at inference time to suppress the target concept without altering model weights. We use embedding regularization strength 0.01 and optimization steps per generation 10 .

sections.heading: SAeUron [ Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ] .
sections.text: SAeUron uses sparse autoencoder feature ablation applied at inference: for each target, τ c \tau_{c} concept-specific SAE features are identified from activation statistics, and these features are zeroed during generation. We use the pre-trained SAE released by the authors, with τ c = 1 \tau_{c}=\textbf{1} features ablated per target.

sections.heading: SLD [ Schramowski et al., 2023 ] .
sections.text: Safe Latent Diffusion adds safety guidance during denoising to suppress target content without retraining the model. Configuration: the SLD-Max preset, i.e. safety guidance scale 5000 , warm-up steps 0 , threshold 1.0 , momentum scale 0.5 , momentum β \beta 0.7 ; 50 sampling steps, CFG scale 7.5 .

sections.heading: SAFREE [ Yoon et al., 2025 ] .
sections.text: SAFREE filters prompt embeddings away from a target-concept subspace and adapts its intervention during denoising without updating model weights. Configuration: concept subspace from 12 per-concept negative terms (synonyms, sub-breeds, and phrasings such as “a photo of a dog”), α \alpha -0.5 , re-attention up to step 20 , FreeU hyperparameters (1.0, 1.0, 0.9, 0.2) ; 50 sampling steps, CFG scale 7.5 .

sections.heading: H.2 Compute and Infrastructure
sections.text: All experiments were run on GPU A100 40GB. Unlearning per method-target pair requires approximately 1 GPU-hours for fine-tuning methods and 2 GPU-hours for inference-time methods. Evaluation (image generation + classification) requires approximately 0.5 GPU-hours per method-target pair.

sections.heading: H.3 Reproducibility
sections.text: For each (method, target) pair, we generate 100 images from direct prompts, 100 to 235 from indirect prompts (depending on how many valid indirect prompts the target yields; 235 for castle , 200 for dog , 195 for horse , and 100 for every other target), 50 per neighbor candidate (500 total), and 50 per control concept (150 total); IRA is computed over the 650 neighbor and control images. All images use fixed random seeds, with seed equal to the row index in the target’s prompt CSV. This ensures seed-level variation is controlled when comparing methods on the same prompt. The base model 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} is loaded from the HuggingFace checkpoint CompVis/stable-diffusion-v1-4 . sections.heading: Appendix I Evaluation Setup and Metric Definitions
sections.text: This appendix provides the full evaluation protocol summarized in Section 5.1 : the prompt construction pipeline for direct, indirect, neighbor, and control evaluation; formal definitions of the six metrics used in Section 5 ; and the classification vocabulary shared across all experiments.

sections.heading: I.1 Prompt Construction and Scoring Pipeline
sections.text: Our automated evaluation protocol is designed to measure two coupled consequences of concept entanglement: indirect recovery , where an erased concept remains recoverable through correlated contextual cues, and collateral forgetting , where suppressing a target concept degrades performance on nearby concepts that should remain intact. To distinguish these effects, we separately construct (i) direct prompts that explicitly name c c , (ii) indirect prompts constructed from correlated context without naming c c , (iii) neighbor prompts that explicitly name each concept in the neighborhood 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{N}(c) , and (iv) control prompts that name each concept in the control set 𝒞 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{C}(c) .

sections.heading: Correlated context extraction.
sections.text: For each target concept c c , we collect a target-matched caption subset from LAION [ Schuhmann et al., 2022 ] aligned with diffusion-model pretraining. Specifically, we identify captions that explicitly contain c c or its lexical variants, and extract co-occurring content words and short phrases from this subset. We remove stopwords, punctuation, low-information function words, and lexical forms that directly mention the target concept. The remaining candidates are ranked using corpus-level association statistics and filtered to obtain a final set of correlated context words that captures the contextual footprint of c c in the training distribution. For example, when c = horse c=\texttt{horse} , the resulting set includes terms such as jockey , stable , saddle , racetrack , and polo , for c = castle c=\texttt{castle} , it includes moat , turret , medieval , knight , and drawbridge . To visualize how these correlated prompts organize in text-embedding space, we pool prompts that explicitly mention the target concept and prompts that omit the target token but retain correlated context, then project their CLIP text embeddings to two dimensions with PCA. Figure 7 shows that context-rich prompts occupy a nearby region rather than a disjoint cluster, supporting our bag-of-words motivation that concept evidence is distributed across correlated tokens rather than isolated in a single concept word. Figure 7: Context-only prompts remain close to target prompts in CLIP text-embedding space. PCA projection of pooled prompts used for the horse case study. One group explicitly contains the concept token, while the other omits it but retains correlated context words (e.g., jockey , saddle , racetrack ). The proximity between these groups illustrates why token-level erasure can remain vulnerable to indirect contextual prompts.

sections.heading: Indirect recovery prompts.
sections.text: We use the correlated context set for c c to construct a set of indirect prompts 𝒫 ind ​ ( c ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ind}}(c) . These prompts are generated under an explicit lexical exclusion constraint: they must not contain the target token or excluded lexical variants of c c . Intuitively, 𝒫 ind ​ ( c ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ind}}(c) probes whether the erased concept can still be elicited through contextual associations alone, without direct lexical mention. To improve prompt diversity while preserving control, we generate multiple prompts from different subsets of the correlated context words and retain only prompts that satisfy the exclusion rule.

sections.heading: Semantic neighbors and control concepts.
sections.text: The semantic neighborhood 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{N}(c) is determined by the procedure of Definition C.1 : 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{N}(c) collects the candidates in c c ’s own pool whose centroid cosine distance to c c falls below the 25th percentile δ c \delta_{c} of pairwise distances in that pool. This produces concept-specific neighborhoods of five to seven discovered neighbors per target ( Table 2 ). The control set 𝒞 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{C}(c) of each target consists of three control concepts drawn from { cactus , jellyfish , melon , police car }, with umbrella in place of police car when the target is car ; these are concepts whose centroids lie well above δ c \delta_{c} for every target, verified to contribute zero to κ ^ \hat{\kappa} across all five targets. For each neighbor c ′ ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}(c) and control c ~ ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( c ) \tilde{c}\in\mathcal{C}(c) , we generate prompts that explicitly mention the concept while excluding lexical forms of the target c c . Per-target prompt files are released in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: Classifier-based scoring.
sections.text: All images are classified using a CLIP-based classifier over a fixed vocabulary of 65 concept labels ( Section I.3 ). For each image, the classifier returns the top-1 label among the vocabulary. All metrics defined below are computed from these top-1 assignments. In several random instances, we also perform a manual evaluation to ensure consistency of the results.

sections.heading: I.2 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Each metric is defined with respect to a base model 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} and an unlearned model 𝒟 θ ^ \mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}} . We write Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 , c , 𝒫 ) \mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D},c,\mathcal{P}) for the fraction of images generated by model 𝒟 \mathcal{D} from prompts in set 𝒫 \mathcal{P} that are classified as concept c c by the CLIP evaluator.

sections.heading: Erasure metrics (measuring ε \varepsilon ).
sections.text: These metrics measure how effectively the target concept c c is suppressed in the unlearned model. • Unlearning Accuracy (UA) : The fraction of images generated from direct prompts 𝒫 dir ​ ( c ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dir}}(c) by 𝒟 θ ^ \mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}} that are not classified as c c . UA ⁡ ( c ) = 1 − Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 θ ^ , c , 𝒫 dir ​ ( c ) ) . \mathrm{UA}(c)=1-\mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}},c,\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dir}}(c)). (25) Higher UA indicates more complete erasure under explicit lexical prompts. • Indirect Recovery Rate (IRR) : The fraction of images generated from indirect recovery prompts 𝒫 ind ​ ( c ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ind}}(c) by 𝒟 θ ^ \mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}} that are classified as c c : IRR ⁡ ( c ) = Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 θ ^ , c , 𝒫 ind ​ ( c ) ) . \mathrm{IRR}(c)=\mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}},c,\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{ind}}(c)). (26) Higher IRR indicates greater vulnerability to concept recovery through correlated contextual cues. In contrast to UA, IRR measures the ε \varepsilon -robust erasure property formalized in Definition 4.2 .

sections.heading: Retention metrics (measuring γ \gamma ).
sections.text: We measure retention at three levels of granularity: • In-domain Retain Accuracy (IRA) : The fraction of images whose intended concept is not the target, i.e., all images from neighbor and control prompts, that are classified as the concept they were meant to show. Direct and indirect recovery prompts are excluded because their intended label is the target itself. IRA therefore measures how well the unlearned model still renders every non-target concept it is asked for, without normalizing by the base model. • Neighbor Preservation (NP) : This is our primary trade-off metric. The overlap with remaining concepts is often dominated by the overlap with a few concepts which are mostly semantically similar with the target concept. Therefore, as a proxy metric for utility preservation, we evaluate utility preservation in the semantic neighborhood 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{N}(c) of the target concept ( Definition C.1 ) and define NP ⁡ ( c ) = 1 | 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) | ​ ∑ c ′ ∈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( c ) Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 θ ^ , c ′ , 𝒫 dir ​ ( c ′ ) ) Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 θ , c ′ , 𝒫 dir ​ ( c ′ ) ) . \mathrm{NP}(c)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(c)|}\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}(c)}\frac{\mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}},c^{\prime},\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dir}}(c^{\prime}))}{\mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D}_{\theta},c^{\prime},\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dir}}(c^{\prime}))}. (27) An NP score of 1.0 1.0 indicates perfect preservation of neighbors after unlearning; lower values indicate proportional collateral damage. The ratio form normalizes out the base-model recognition accuracy, which differs across concepts (and which is generally below 1.0 under a 65-class vocabulary). • Control preservation (CP) : To distinguish neighbor-specific collateral damage from broader degradation, we additionally evaluate performance on a non-neighbor control set 𝒞 ⁡ ( c ) \mathcal{C}(c) . We define CP ⁡ ( c ) = 1 | 𝒞 ⁡ ( c ) | ​ ∑ c ~ ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ( c ) Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 θ ^ , c ~ , 𝒫 dir ​ ( c ~ ) ) Acc ⁡ ( 𝒟 θ , c ~ , 𝒫 dir ​ ( c ~ ) ) . \mathrm{CP}(c)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}(c)|}\sum_{\tilde{c}\in\mathcal{C}(c)}\frac{\mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}},\tilde{c},\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tilde{c}))}{\mathrm{Acc}(\mathcal{D}_{\theta},\tilde{c},\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tilde{c}))}. (28) Comparing NP and CP isolates neighbor-specific collateral damage from broader degradation: a method with NP ≪ CP \mathrm{NP}\ll\mathrm{CP} is damaging concepts selectively in the target’s neighborhood, consistent with the propagation mechanism in Theorem 4.6 . A method with NP ≈ CP ≪ 1 \mathrm{NP}\approx\mathrm{CP}\ll 1 is causing uniform degradation across the concept space.

sections.heading: DamageGap.
sections.text: A summary statistic we introduce to quantify neighbor-selective damage: DamageGap ⁡ ( c ) = CP ⁡ ( c ) − NP ⁡ ( c ) \mathrm{DamageGap}(c)=\mathrm{CP}(c)-\mathrm{NP}(c) . A positive DamageGap indicates that neighbors are damaged more than controls, consistent with the trade-off predicted by Theorem 4.6 . A DamageGap near zero indicates uniform degradation (or uniform preservation) across both sets.

sections.heading: Appendix N Broader Impacts
sections.text: Our analysis is instantiated in diffusion models, but the mechanism only requires activation displacement, local smoothness of the activation map, and target-neighbor overlap in representation space. We show that these failure modes stem from the geometry of concept representations rather than from any particular algorithm. Formalizing concepts as activation-space regions, we prove that the overlap between a target and other concepts lower-bounds the damage any robust erasure must inflict on them, with the trade-off scaling linearly in the degree of overlap. Across thirteen unlearning methods, including methods designed to preserve non-target concepts, no method achieves both strong erasure and strong neighbor preservation: STEREO nearly eliminates indirect leakage but cuts neighbor generation by more than 75%, while sparse inference-time methods preserve neighbors but leak. Damage increases with our overlap measure, monotonically so for STEREO; the κ \kappa -scaling reproduces on SDXL, and neighbor-selective damage recurs on FLUX. Perfect unlearning is the wrong target for entangled concepts; methods should be evaluated on the Pareto frontier our theorem establishes. 1 Introduction Text-to-image diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) have rapidly become the dominant generative paradigm for high-fidelity image synthesis, with deployments ranging from creative tools to commercial APIs. Privacy concerns and copyrights have motivated active research on concept unlearning ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) : given a trained model and an undesirable concept (e.g., an object category, an artistic style, or a specific identity), the goal is to suppress the concept while preserving the model’s general capabilities. In this work, we focus on object-category concepts, where benchmarks and detectors are most mature. A growing body of work has proposed methods for this task, ranging from fine-tuning-based approaches that permanently alter model weights ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Fan et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) to inference-time interventions that block concept-specific activations without modifying the underlying model ( Li et al., 2024 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ; Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) . These methods are typically evaluated on two families of metrics: unlearning accuracy (UA), measuring whether the target concept has been successfully suppressed, and retain accuracy (RA), measuring whether the model’s performance on non-target concepts remains intact. A tacit assumption in this evaluation paradigm is that UA and RA can be optimized independently. However, our empirical evidence suggests this assumption is violated ( Section 3 ). Methods achieving strong erasure (high UA), such as STEREO ( Srivatsan et al., 2025 ) , often degrade generation quality on semantically related concepts (low RA). Methods with better retention, such as SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) , leave the target concept reachable through prompts that omit its name but supply correlated context (e.g., generating a horse from “a jockey at the racetrack”), a phenomenon we call concept leakage , resulting in low UA. These observations indicate a fundamental tension: unlearning and retention are inherently coupled when concepts share representational structure , a coupling visible directly in the model’s internal representations, where semantically related concepts ( horse / pony / donkey ) occupy overlapping regions of activation space while isolated concepts ( castle ) sit well-separated ( Figure 1 ). This shows that concept activation regions are real geometric structures whose overlap reflects semantic similarity, motivating our formal notion of concept activation regions in Section 4 1 1 1 The formal definition of concept activation regions is in Appendix A ; full empirical construction details and per-concept clustering statistics are in Appendix B . . Two failure modes follow from this geometry: concept leakage , where the target concept reappears under indirect prompts, and collateral forgetting , degraded generation of semantically related but distinct concepts. We show that these are not shortcomings of individual algorithms but dual symptoms of overlapping concept regions, and that any robust erasure method must trade them off.
