Contributions. (i) We give a geometric account of concept entanglement, showing that the literature’s two failure modes, concept leakage and collateral forgetting, are dual symptoms of overlapping concept regions in cross-attention activation space (quantified by an entanglement coefficient κ ^ \hat{\kappa} ), rather than separate algorithmic shortcomings as treated in prior work ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Srivatsan et al., 2025 ; Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) . (ii) Building on this account, we derive a geometric lower-bound for concept unlearning under empirically-verified assumptions: any method achieving ε \varepsilon -robust erasure must incur utility preservation error γ ≥ κ ⁡ ( 1 − ε ) / L \gamma\geq\kappa(1-\varepsilon)/L ( Theorem 4.6 ), with strict impossibility at ε = 0 \varepsilon=0 whenever κ > 0 \kappa>0 ( Corollary 4.8 ); this result reframes unlearning as a Pareto problem rather than a dual-objective one. (iii) We validate the predicted κ \kappa -scaled trade-off across thirteen methods on Stable Diffusion v1.4 (all methods on five targets, four methods on five additional targets that fill the intermediate κ ^ \hat{\kappa} range), with κ \kappa -scaling reproduced on SDXL, using a new Neighbor Preservation metric tied to the activation-level γ \gamma in our theorem. 2 Related Work Machine unlearning in diffusion models aims to remove a target concept c c (e.g., horse ) from a pretrained model 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} while preserving overall generative capabilities. The goal is an updated model 𝒟 θ ^ \mathcal{D}_{\hat{\theta}} that suppresses c c on target-associated prompts while maintaining quality on unrelated prompts, following prior work on concept erasure in diffusion models. Background on latent diffusion models is in Appendix A.1 . Closed-form editing. UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) and RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) modify cross-attention projections through analytic updates, without gradient training. RECE additionally searches for embeddings that regenerate the target and removes them in closed form. Fine-tuning methods. A large body of work erase concepts by directly modifying the weights of a pretrained diffusion model. Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) Gandikota et al. (2023) uses negative guidance to align target-token prompts with a neutral anchor. Subsequent work improves the precision by editing cross-attention representations ( Wang et al., 2025 ) or updating salient concept-related parameters ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Wu and Harandi, 2024 ) . CPE ( Lee et al., 2025 ) trains residual attention gates with an anchoring loss, and TRUST ( Kori et al., 2026 ) selectively fine-tunes target-associated neurons under Hessian-based regularization. More recent robust methods such as AdvUnlearn Zhang et al. (2024) and STEREO Srivatsan et al. (2025) further defend against prompt-based regeneration attacks. However, these methods still largely define erasure through target tokens, prompts, or localized parameter subsets. They therefore suppress direct target prompts well, but struggle with concept leakage through correlated context; when made more aggressive, their edits can propagate through shared representations and cause collateral damage to semantic neighbors. Inference-time methods. A complementary line of work avoids modifying 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} and instead intervenes during generation by manipulating text embeddings ( Li et al., 2024 ) , projecting prompt tokens away from a target subspace (SAFREE, Yoon et al., 2025 ), adding safety guidance to the denoising process (SLD, Schramowski et al., 2023 ), inserting lightweight concept-blocking adapters ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , or ablating sparse-autoencoder features ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) . These methods are computationally efficient and often preserve broad model behavior. Intervening at inference time does not by itself make a method conservative: depending on how broadly the intervention displaces activations, these methods span the full range from strong erasure with substantial neighbor damage to strong preservation with residual leakage (Section 5.2 ). Preservation-oriented methods. Several methods explicitly target the collateral damage we study. CPE anchors non-target concepts during erasure, TRUST restricts updates to target-associated neurons, and SAFREE adapts its filtering to preserve prompt fidelity. Adversarial preservation ( Bui et al., 2024 ) identifies and protects the concepts most sensitive to erasure, Receler ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) localize edits through lightweight erasers and LoRA fusion, and meta-unlearning ( Gao et al., 2025 ) prevents relearning of erased concepts. We evaluate CPE, TRUST, and SAFREE; they reach more favorable operating points but do not escape the trade-off (Section 5.2 ). Positioning. That aggressive erasure degrades utility is well documented, and the preservation-oriented methods above aim to reduce it; localization work such as Zarei et al. (2026) identifies where concepts are represented. Neither models target-neighbor overlap or derives limits on unlearning. Our claim is narrower and structural: robust erasure necessarily degrades related concepts because their representations overlap, a limit we quantify through κ \kappa , prove unavoidable (Theorem 4.6 , Corollary 4.8 ), and turn into a frontier-based evaluation protocol. Across all three families, methods implicitly treat concepts as localized and independently suppressible; this assumption fails whenever activation regions overlap. 3 Motivation Current concept unlearning methods are designed to suppress a concept token (e.g., “ horse ”) so as to remove the corresponding visual concept without substantially affecting other concepts. This design implicitly assumes that visual concepts are represented as localized, token-aligned features in the model’s joint text-image space. In this section, we present empirical evidence that this assumption fails: in practice, unlearning a target concept produces collateral damage to the concepts with which it is entangled. 2 2 2 We define entanglement formally in Section 4.1 based on activation regions in the model’s cross-attention space. The severity of this damage is coupled to both the strength of the erasure applied to the target concept and the extent of its entanglement with other concepts. This coupling is the phenomenon our theoretical framework analyzes in Section 4 . The training mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models make entanglement inevitable. First, diffusion models condition on prompt embeddings produced by text encoders that often exhibit bag-of-words behavior ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2022 ) . As a result, prompts that omit a concept token (e.g., horse ) but retain its characteristic context (e.g., jockey , saddle , racetrack ) can still induce activations associated with that concept (see Figure 7 ). This implies that the visual concept is not localized in a single token, but is instead distributed across multiple correlated context tokens. Second, semantically related concepts share much of this contextual structure (e.g., a horse in a field” vs. a donkey in a field” ), which leads to overlapping activation regions in the model’s internal representation space. Whether this overlap is already present in text space depends on the encoder. Under our estimator, SDXL’s CLIP text embeddings place nine of ten concepts in overlapping regions, whereas the T5 encoder of FLUX shows no measurable overlap for any of our five targets (Appendix L ). Entanglement in the denoiser therefore need not be inherited from the text encoder; its source and severity depend on both the text representation and the denoiser computation. We treat this comparison as descriptive rather than as a causal decomposition. Figure 2 illustrates an example of the trade-off due to this entanglement. It shows two unlearning methods using horse as the erasure target. Method that perform localized erasure (ESD Gandikota et al. (2023) ) successfully suppress generation when the target token is named, but regenerate the concept through indirect prompts that name only context words, which we call concept leakage . Methods that erase more aggressively (STEREO Srivatsan et al. (2025) ) suppress this leakage but produce visibly degraded outputs for some semantically similar concepts, such as donkey and zebra , that are entangled with the target concept (see Figure 1 ). We call this effect collateral damage . Table 1 quantifies this coupling.
